copy source: the start-up copies these bytes to $CAD0, where they are described; nothing reads them here afterwards
runtime: the game's variables (named in the listing), zero in the file
runtime: variables between the two bank switches at $623F and $624A
runtime: the game's variables and tables (named in the listing), zero in the file; the start-up clears $679D-$77D4 again at $4BCE

filler at the end of the program file, as at $909D
the top of the resource heap, which nothing has loaded into at start-up; rooms, scripts, costumes and sounds come in from the disk during play
runtime: a work area below the code at $CAD0, zero after the start-up and written in play

runtime: the game's variables under the KERNAL (named in the listing), set by the start-up and written as it runs

comments.text: The four bytes a stream names as its commonest, for decode_byte's short runs; copied from the stream's start by decode_start

Starts decoding the stream at $26/$27: its first four bytes are the commonest bytes, kept at $0100-$0103, and the decoder is set with no run under way. The decoder lives here, in the stack page, copied from $823C at start-up

The next byte of the stream, Y kept. A code byte below $40 is followed by that many bytes plus one, as they are; $40 to $7F repeat the byte after it its low six bits plus one times; $80 and over repeat one of the four common bytes (bits 5 and 6) its low five bits plus one times
The byte at $26/$27, the pointer then moved on
Decodes and throws away the number of bytes in $2D/$2E. Nothing in the program calls it
Decodes and throws away $2D bytes (none when it is zero)
Not used: the byte after the decoder

Plays a sound for an actor in the room: for each of the four actor slots whose flag in $FD52 is set, when the actor has a sound ($FF83) starts it (start_sound, with no slot current) and clears all four flags; one sound at most

After a pass that redrew the room, when the room is lit (bit 1 of variable 12): asks the frame interrupt to show the screen just drawn and points $23/$24 at the other one for the next: after drawing on $CC00 ($22 = 1) it asks for $CC00 ($21 = 2) and draws next on $C800, and the other way round
Entry from $D639: asks for the screen at $CC00 and makes $C800 the one to draw on next
Fatal error 4, out of memory in the heap ($D472): the border changes colour for ever
Seven bytes after the endless loop: $FF and six zeros, which nothing reads
An RTS the main loop calls on every pass

Called each pass: when $FC2D is 1 (a click with nothing under the cursor, at $27CF) clears it, and when the cursor is hidden (bit 4 of user_state clear) or variable 32, the click area, is 4, starts global script 4

Draws the sentence line, row 18 at $CED0: clears it, then, when the interface shows the sentence (bit 5 of user_state), writes the verb's name (variable 26, the verb_name_pointer), the first object's (27), the preposition's (29, from the table at $F0C1/$F0C6) and the second object's (28), each followed by a space, cut at 40 characters
Points $15/$16 at the name of verb A: finds the verb's slot (21 to 0) in $F149 and takes its name block from $77C1/$779E (four bytes on, past the header); with no name, an empty string at $F0C0

Points $15/$16 at the name of the object or actor in X (low) and A (high): an actor (A 0 and X no more than variable 11, the number of actors) has its name block ($77B4/$7791); an object has the name in its record, at the offset in its byte 14 (find_object); with no name, the empty string at $F0C0

Finds object X (low) and A (high): looks its owner up in the object table at $6B47 (into $0913); an object owned by an actor is looked for among the inventory's 60 slots ($679D numbers, $67D9/$6815 addresses) and returns A 0 with $15/$16 its record; an object in the room ($0F) among the room's objects ($6A2F/$6A0C numbers), and returns A 1 with Y its index, $17/$18 its offset in the room and $15/$16 its record. Not found: $FF
find_object with the object already in $15/$16
The table's address is written into this LDA's operand at $0770 and $0777
Clears screen row 18 ($CED0, 40 bytes) to zero
Copies the name at $15/$16 onto the sentence row at $19/$1A, skipping $40 characters, up to its zero and no further than column 40 ($0912 counts), and moves $19/$1A past it
Finds the object in $15/$16 and returns its preposition, the top three bits of its byte 12, with Y left at 12; $FF when the object is not found

Each pass of the main loop, when the sentence script (global script 2) is not running and a sentence is queued: takes the newest from the queue; one whose two objects are the same is dropped; otherwise its verb and objects go to variables 8, 9 and 10, the verb's entry in the first object's verb table to variable 18, and global script 2 is started to carry it out

The position of the object or actor in X (low) and A (high) in $FC18/$FC19: an actor's from its walk record when it is in the room ($FF when it is not); an object in the inventory, its owner's; an object in the room, its walk-to point ($69A3, $69C6 times 4) and the direction to face ($69E9, into $FC1A), moved to the nearest point a walk box allows ($17DC). $FF when not found, 0 when found
The sentence row's column, counted by append_name
The owner of the object find_object looked up last (the low four bits of its byte in the object table)

For walkActorToActor: a point beside the second actor (Y), on the first actor's side (X): the distance the opcode gave added to the second actor's X when the first is to its right, taken from it when it is to its left ($0933 and $0938 are the two ADC operands), with 8 added when that goes below zero; the second actor's Y; then moved into a walk box as object_or_actor_xy does
The newest entry in the sentence queue, $FF when it is empty
The sentence run_verb_script carries out now: its verb, the first object ($094F/$0950) and the second ($0952/$0953)

The sentence queue, six entries: the verbs; then the first objects' low bytes ($095A) and high bytes ($0960), whether there is a second object ($0966), and the second objects' low bytes ($096C) and high bytes ($0972)
Copies the zero-ended string at $15/$16 into the message buffer at $0200 from X on, leaving out $40 characters; X ends past it
For a message's escape code: the next byte of the text names a variable holding an object's number; that object's name goes into the message
For a message's escape code: the text that starts at the variable the next byte names (in the variables' low bytes from $FE6E) goes into the message
For a message's escape code: the value of the variable the next byte names goes into the message in decimal

Writes the 16-bit number in $0A50/$0A51 into the message buffer in decimal: counts how many times each power of ten from the table at $0A47 goes into it, leaving out zeros before the first digit; the last digit is always written
Writes digit A into the message buffer as its character ($30 plus A), unless it is a leading zero ($0A52 still 0)
The powers of ten print_decimal divides by, as words: 10000, 1000, 100, 10
Where print_decimal writes next in the message buffer
The number print_decimal writes, low and high bytes
0 until print_decimal has written its first digit, so zeros before it are left out

Saves the game on the disk in the drive: refuses a game disk (check_game_disk); writes $5A, the mark of a save disk, to block 1, then the script variables and the state after them ($FD6F, $283 bytes) to block 5, seven bytes from $00B6 to block 6, the verbs' table ($F0D9, $A0 bytes) to block 7, and everything from $679D to the end of the heap ($6063 bytes) from block 8. Returns 0
Loads a saved game: refuses a game disk; returns 2 when block 1 does not hold the mark $5A; otherwise reads the same blocks back where save_game took them from, and returns 3

Reads the first byte of block 1 into $15; when it is "0", "1" or "2", the disk is one of the game's own: it drops its caller's return address, so the save or load returns 1 at once. Otherwise returns 0
The X positions of the four actor sprites for this frame, low bytes ($0B66-$0B69), copied in by the frame interrupt from $1174-$1177
The cursor sprite's X position (sprite 7), low byte
The colours of the four actor sprites ($0B6E-$0B71), used when bit 3 of the lights is set; and four more bytes, 4 to 7, that nothing reads
The cursor sprite's colour, stepped through the greys at $1167 by the frame interrupt
Which hardware sprite (0 to 3) draws each of the four actor slots ($0B76-$0B79), copied from $1178-$117B; the four bytes after them, 3 to 6, are not read
Bit 8 of each actor sprite's X position ($0B7D-$0B80), copied from $1170-$1173
Bit 8 of the cursor sprite's X position
The X high bits of all the sprites, put together by arm_raster_chain for $D010
The sprites' X expansion ($D01D), set by the raster interrupt at $0C1C
The cursor sprite's Y position
Where each raster interrupt keeps Y while it runs ($0B89 A, $0B8A X)
The four actor sprites' X positions by hardware sprite, two bytes apart ($0B8B, $0B8D, $0B8F, $0B91), which the room's interrupt writes to $D000-$D006; the bytes between are not read

Starts the raster interrupt chain for the next frame: puts the four actor sprites' X high bits (each shifted to its hardware sprite's bit) and the cursor's into $D010, sets the cursor's X, and asks for an interrupt at line $29, handled at $0C1C

The raster interrupt at line $29, above the picture: banks the chips in, sets each actor sprite's X for the room and the X expansion, writes the first band's sprite pointers (from $1156, one for each of the four sprites) into the shown screen's pointer table ($78/$79), sets the cursor's pointer ($115E) on both screens, the actor sprites' colours (their own when bit 3 of the lights is set, otherwise dark grey) and the cursor's colour and Y, puts sprites 0 to 3 at Y $32 and asks for line $42 ($0D15)

The raster interrupt at line $42, where the picture starts: multicolour text from the room's screen and character set ($AB into $D018, $D016 = $18), the actor sprites' X positions and high bits; after a delay of NOPs moves sprites 0 to 3 down to the next band, Y $47, writes that band's pointers ($1157) and asks for line $4F ($0DBA)
Line $4F: moves the actor sprites down to Y $5C, the third band, and asks for line $59 ($0DF2)
Line $59: the third band's sprite pointers, from $1158; asks for line $63 ($0E46)
Line $63: the actor sprites to Y $71; asks for line $6D ($0E7E)
Line $6D: the fourth band's pointers, from $1159; asks for line $77 ($0ED2)
Line $77: the actor sprites to Y $86; asks for line $81 ($0F0A)
Line $81: the fifth band's pointers, from $115A; asks for line $8B ($0F5E)
Line $8B: the actor sprites to Y $9B; asks for line $95 ($0F96)
Line $95: the sixth band's pointers, from $115B; asks for line $9F ($0FEA)
Line $9F: the actor sprites to Y $B0; asks for line $A9 ($1022)
Line $A9: the seventh band's pointers, from $115C; asks for line $B1 ($1076)
Line $B1: the actor sprites to Y $C5, the last band; asks for line $BD ($10AE)
Line $BD: the last band's pointers, from $115D; asks for line $C3 ($1102)

Line $C3, below the picture: hires text from the screen at $CC00 and the character set at $F800 ($D018 = $3E, $D016 = $09) for the sentence line, the verbs and the inventory; moves the actor sprites off the bottom (Y $FD) and asks for line $FB, the frame interrupt at $117C
The first sprite pointer of each of the eight bands ($1156-$115D), four consecutive pointers a band: $A0 to $BC for the sprites at $E800, or $80 to $9C for the other buffer at $E000
The cursor's sprite pointer: $C1 normally, $C2 while the disk is read (busy_cursor)
Set by the main loop when it has drawn the actors into a sprite buffer: 1 for the one at $E000 (pointers $80 up), 2 for $E800; the frame interrupt switches to it and clears this
Cleared by the frame interrupt; $D748 waits on it
1 while the cursor is hidden (set_user_state); the frame interrupt then neither moves nor shows it
The cursor's state to come back to, set with $1161
The countdown between steps of the cursor's colour, reloaded from $1165
Which colour of the six at $1167 the cursor shows, counting down from $1166
Frames between the cursor's colour steps, 6
The last of the cursor's colours, 5 (six colours, 0 to 5)
The cursor's colours, stepped through by the frame interrupt: white, light grey, grey, dark grey, grey, light grey
Set when the frame interrupt has copied the room's colours this frame (copy_room_colours); the cursor is not moved that frame
Set while the frame interrupt's slow part runs, so that an interrupt arriving before it ends leaves at once
Set by busy_cursor: bit 0 stops the timers and the cursor's colours, bit 1 the music, while the disk is read
The next frame's actor sprite X high bits ($1170-$1173), set by the actor drawing code and copied into $0B7D by the frame interrupt
The next frame's actor sprite X positions ($1174-$1177)
The next frame's hardware sprite for each actor slot ($1178-$117B)

The raster interrupt at line $FB, once a frame: keeps the registers and the bank, counts the frame counters $C6 and $1F; when the main loop has a new frame ready ($7A), switches to the sprite buffer it drew ($115F) with its X positions and sprite numbers, rearms the raster chain, and shows the screen it drew ($21: 1 the screen at $C800, 2 the one at $CC00, each with the room's character set at $D800; 3 only the colours), copying the room's colours into colour RAM (copy_room_colours). Then, with interrupts allowed again: counts down the timers $FC20/$FC21 and $B8/$B9, the scripts' delays (count_script_delays) and the cursor's colour, reads the joystick and keyboard ($1BAF), moves the cursor ($F1F3, $F28E) unless it is hidden or the interface is being redrawn, takes this frame's click ($FC13) and plays the music and sounds ($3FE0)
copy_room_colours with the chips banked in
Copies the room's colours, 16 rows of 40 from the buffer at $64F5, into colour RAM rows 2 to 17 ($D850), and sets $116D
Shows the snail (cursor pointer $C2) and keeps A in $116F, which stops the timers, the cursor's colours or the music while the disk works; the cursor's colour becomes white
The arrow again: cursor pointer $C1 and $116F cleared

Unless the music player runs ($43E8) or the picture is off already ($82): waits for the frame interrupt to clear $D0, then turns interrupts off, the screen and the sprites off and the border black, and silences the sound when $43E0 asks; sets $82

When the picture is off ($82): turns the sprites and the screen on, puts the frame interrupt ($117C) in the IRQ vector, asks for line $FA, clears and enables the raster interrupt, gives the sound its volume back ($43DE) when it was silenced, allows interrupts and clears $82
Set by video_off when it silenced the sound, so that video_on gives the volume back

Direction tables for walk boxes whose flags change how an actor faces (flags' low three bits): this first 32 bytes give, for the way the actor moves (row: 0 right and down, 1 right and up... from the signs at $FD3E/$FD42) and the box's flags (column), the column to use in the next table
For a walking actor: its new direction, by its direction (row of eight) and the column from the table at $147A
For a standing actor: its new direction, by its direction (row of eight) and the box's flags (column)
Changes the direction in $FD16 for the walk box the actor stands in, through the tables at $147A-$14D9, chosen by the box's flags ($24DE) and, while it walks, by the way it moves

One step of the walking actor in slot $C5 (actor $E5), each frame: while it turns (bit 7 of $FCF6) it turns a quarter at a time towards its new direction through the table at $1936 and shows each turn; while it walks (bit 0): at the start of each leg (bit 2) either stops, at the last (bit 1), or moves to the next walk box on the way to the destination box (next_box), checks that box is allowed (check_box_allowed), finds where to cross into it (box_crossing_point) and starts the leg (start_leg); between, it takes a step (step_actor)
The next walk box on the way from the actor's box ($FD06) to its destination box ($FD0E), from the room's box matrix (box_matrix_pointer)

For a box whose flags (A) have bit 6 set the walk stops at its edge (bit 1 set, no direction to face at the end): for every actor, or, when bit 5 is set as well, only for the actors from variable 42 to variable 43

Stops the actor in slot $C5: only bit 7 of $FCF6 kept, its standing animation for the direction it faces ($FC1B = direction + 4, start_animation), then turns it to its final direction ($FD02) when it has one
Where the actor crosses into the next box: the point of the next box nearest the actor ($24EB), then the point of the current box nearest that ($24EB again), left in $2670/$2671

Starts a leg of the walk towards the point in $192B/$192C: works out the step (setup_leg; none to take ends the leg at once), turns the actor when the leg goes another way (left, right, or up and down when it is steeper), starts its walking animation for the direction ($208A) unless it shows it already ($FD12), and takes the first step unless it is turning
Moves the actor one step along its leg, X and Y each by a line-drawing count (step_axis, called for X and again four bytes on for Y), and marks the leg done (bit 2 of $FCF6) when it reaches the point
Points $17/$18 at the room's box matrix index (after the walk boxes, eight bytes each, from $24A3) and $15/$16 at the matrix itself, one row for each box after the index

The screen position of the actor in slot $C5's sprite column: X (its column less the camera's, $CBC0, plus 3, times 8, plus 1, less 1) in $FCDE with bit 8 in $FCE2, and Y (its Y less its height above the floor, times 2, plus 2) in $FCDA

Sends actor $E5 walking to $FC18/$FC19, facing $FC1A at the end ($FF: any). An actor not in the room is put there at once. Otherwise the point is moved into the nearest walk box (adjust_to_box); when the actor is there already, facing the right way, nothing happens; otherwise the destination, the final direction, the destination box and the start box are filed and the walk starts (bits 0 and 2 of $FCF6)
Moves the point $FC33/$FC34 in room $FC35 to the nearest point inside a walk box ($23FD) and returns the box in A; $FF when the room is not the one shown

When the camera has moved: runs $35A9 for every actor in the room and $3491, then, for each of the four slots with a sprite ($FD2E) that is not being redrawn or walking, works out its sprite's new X position (actor_sprite_position) for the next frame ($1174/$1170)

The line from the actor to its waypoint ($FCEE/$FCF2): the X and Y distances ($1930, $192F), their directions ($1934, $1935: 1 to the right or down) and the larger ($192E) into the slot's step counts ($FD32-$FD4A), with $1933 set when the line is steeper than flat. Carry set when there is nowhere to go

One axis of a step: adds the axis's distance ($FD46) to its count ($FD36); when the count reaches the larger distance, takes that off and moves the position ($FCE6) one towards the waypoint. Called with X the slot for X and the slot plus four for Y, whose tables lie four bytes further on
The point the next leg goes to, X and Y ($192C)
The slot update_actor_sprites works on
The larger of the two distances of a leg, which each step's count is measured against
The leg's Y distance; $1930 its X distance
The X and Y counts' starting values ($1932 for Y)
1 when the leg is steeper than flat, so the actor faces up or down
1 when the leg goes right; $1935 1 when it goes down
The direction to turn to next, by the direction faced (row of four) and the one wanted (column): turns go a quarter at a time

Draws one picture of a costume, at $6E/$6F, into the actor's sprite column at $FC03/$FC04. Its header gives its width in bytes (four pixels each), its height in rows, its X offset in bytes and its Y offset above the row in $35; it is fatal error 7 when the width or height is zero or the picture would be wider than the column's three bytes. Rows above the column or below its 137th are skipped. The picture is stored a column at a time, top to bottom, in runs: a byte with bit 7 clear counts the bytes that follow, one with bit 7 set counts repeats of the one byte after it, and a repeated zero leaves those rows untouched. Each byte is masked in with the table at $1AA4, so colour 0 lets what is behind show. For an actor facing left ($FC02) the picture is drawn mirrored: from the right-hand byte leftwards, each byte through the table at $D200 that reverses its four pixels
This instruction (and the one at $1A47) is written by $19C7: LDA $D200,Y, which mirrors the byte, for a mirrored picture, or LDY $D200, which leaves the byte in A as it is
This instruction (and those at $1A82 and $1A9C) is written by $19CD as INC or DEC, so a mirrored picture is drawn from right to left
The mask for each multicolour byte value, 256 bytes: %11 in each pair of bits that is %00, where colour 0 shows what is behind, and %00 in each pair that holds a colour
The keyboard's column lines read from $DC01 with every row driven low; $1BA6 the row lines read from $DC00 the other way round
More than one key in the column read (zero: exactly one); $1BA7 the same for the rows
The number of the bit found low by count_low_bits; $1BA9 keeps the column's
The key reported last, $FF when none is held: a key held down is reported once
$40 while a shift key is held, added to the key table's index to read its shifted half
The held shift key's column bit; $1BAD its row bit, taken out of the next scan so the other key can be read
1 when a key is waiting in $2F

Each frame, from the frame interrupt: reads the joystick in port 1 (read_joystick); a move or the button, or a cut-scene running ($FF6F), sets the idle count at $FC20/$FC21 back to 18,000 frames. When the count has run out (the frame interrupt counts it down), files the space bar, which pauses the game. Then scans the keyboard: drives every row low and reads the columns, then the other way round, so that one key gives one low bit each way, and turns column and row into an index into the key table at $1CF8 (column times 8 plus row, plus $40 shifted). Two keys at once are read only when one is a shift key. A new key goes into $2F with $1BAE set
A key to report (A not zero): into $2F, with $1BAE set
Two keys at once: when one of them is a shift key, its bits are taken out of the column and row read and the scan is made again; otherwise the keys are ignored
Counts the low bits of A and keeps the number of the lowest in $1BA8; returns the count less one: 0 for exactly one key, $FF (negative) for none
Not used: one byte left over after count_low_bits
Reads joystick port 1 ($DC01, with port A's lines all driven high so no keyboard row is selected) into $31; Z is set when it is neither moved nor fired (the low five bits all 1)
Not used: one byte left over before the key table

The key each position of the keyboard's matrix gives, by column (eight rows of eight): letters and digits as ASCII, RETURN $0D, space $20, F1 to F7 $01 to $04, the cursor keys $C8 to $CD, a shift key $7B (left) or $7D (right), and $5F for a key the game ignores. This first half is unshifted
The shifted half: shifted F1 to F7 give $05 to $08 (shifted F1 saves and loads, shifted F7 restarts), the shifted digits their symbols
Waits until a key is pressed and returns it. Nothing in the program calls it
The waiting key in A and $1BAE cleared, or zero when none is waiting

Draws the next frame of actor $E5, in walk slot $C5, into its sprite column: once its costume is found (costume_pointer) and checked ($57 as its second byte), loads the slot's animation state, works out the sprite's column on the screen ($FC0C), clears the rows the last frame in this buffer used, draws every limb (draw_limbs), keeps the rows this frame used, masks it behind the room's foreground when it stands behind something ($FD1A), copies the seam rows (copy_seam_rows), hands the sprite's X position and the actor's colour to the raster interrupt ($1170, $1174, $0B6E) and saves the animation state

Draws the eight limbs of actor X's costume, each picture placed from the row in $35 (the sprite's foot) and mirrored when the actor faces left (direction 0, $FC02). The limbs' frame lists start at the costume's word at offset 2. When any limb is still animating ($2088), the slot is drawn again next frame

Advances limb $FC0B to its next frame and draws it: a limb that loops (bit 7 of its frame clear) goes back to its first frame after the last; one that plays once holds its last; $FF is a limb not shown. The frame's entry in the frame list gives the picture, with bit 7 asking for the actor's sound ($FD52); the limb's own table (at the costume's word at offset 4 plus twice the limb) gives the picture's address. Each picture's bytes 4 and 5 move the next one: X right by the first, Y up by the second (place_next_picture)

When the last picture asked for a move ($FC00 X, $FC01 Y), adds it to the position ($34, and $35 less the Y move); otherwise keeps the last position ($FC11/$FC12). Leaves it in $34/$35 and $FC11/$FC12. The drawer itself uses only $35 and each picture's own X offset
Points $DD/$DE at actor $E5's costume, past the resource's four-byte header, from the costumes' address table ($741B low, $73F5 high bytes)

Copies slot $C5's 32 bytes of animation state from $FC5A-$FCD9 to the working copy at $FC3A-$FC59: for each of eight limbs its frame (with bit 7 for play once), its first frame ($FC42), its last ($FC4A) and its animation ($FC52)
Copies the working animation state at $FC3A-$FC59 back to slot $C5's 32 bytes

Clears, in sprite Y's column, the rows the last frame drawn into this buffer used (from its height, $3604 or $360C, up to its foot, $3600 or $3608), kept apart for the two buffers ($FC0E), clipped to the column's 137 rows
Keeps the foot ($35) and height ($FC38) of the frame just drawn for sprite Y in this buffer, for clear_old_rows next time, and the height for the slot ($FD26)

The address of sprite Y's column in the buffer being drawn ($FC0E: $E000 when set, $E800 when clear), into $FC03/$FC04: the sprite's 64-byte block in the first band, from the tables at $206A and $2072

The raster interrupt switches each band's sprite pointer to the next band's block three lines before the band ends, so the chip reads a band's last rows from the next block. For each of the seven rows where the switch happens (the rows at $207A), copies its three bytes into the block 256 bytes before as well, so it shows the same whichever block the chip reads
$70/$71: the address of row Y of the sprite column at $FC03/$FC04, through the row tables at $D3B0 and $D310
$6E/$6F: the address 256 bytes before $70/$71, in the band before
The low byte of each sprite's column, for sprites 0 to 7; $2072 the high bytes' offset, before $E0 or $E8 is added
The seven rows of the sprite column where the pointer moves to the next band's block, 20 rows apart
For each walk slot, the offset of the last of its 32 bytes in the animation state at $FC5A
The limb's frame; $2086 its last frame; $2087 its play once flag (bit 7)
Counts the limbs still animating in the frame being drawn
X kept while clear_old_rows and copy_seam_rows work

Starts animation $FC1B on actor $E5, when it has a costume and is in the room: the slot is redrawn twice. The costume's second byte must be $57, or it is fatal error 2 (the border flashes). Animations $F8 to $FB only turn the actor to the direction in their low two bits; others beyond the costume's count (its first byte) are ignored. Otherwise each limb the animation names starts it (start_animation_limbs), and limbs showing an animation for another direction turn with it (turn_limbs)

The size asked for, kept while the heap is compacted ($4752 high)

X/Y: bytes 2 and 3 of the block at $3F/$40, a free block's link to the next

The size of the first free block, while the heap is compacted ($4821 high)
The size of the block being moved ($4823 high)
The next free block after the first ($4825 high): the blocks up to it are moved down
The type of the block being moved; $4827 its number

Moves each block in use, from just after the first free block up to the next free one, down to the first free block's address: copies it (copy_block) and tells its owner where it is now (move_resource_address). A sound that is playing is marked while it moves ($FC31 bit 0), so the music's code knows. Then writes the free block's header after them
Sets bit 0 of $FC31 while a sound that is playing is moved
Clears bit 0 of $FC31 again

Writes a block's new address ($3F/$40) into its owner's table, by its type (Y) and number (X): 1 an inventory object ($67D9/$6815), 2 a costume ($741B/$73F5), 3 a room ($73BA/$737F), 4 a block of the room's graphics ($77B2/$778F), 5 a script ($7659/$75BE), 6 a sound ($74C0/$7441). Any other type is fatal error 5

Throws out resources that are loaded and not in use, one kind at a time, starting after the kind tried last ($FC1E): the oldest room, a costume, every sound, every script. Returns $FF as soon as something has been freed ($FC1D, set by free_block), 0 when a whole round found nothing
Frees the room that has gone longest unshown ($7344, which grows by one each time another room is entered) and is not locked (bit 7), of rooms 1 to 58
Frees the first costume, from 37 down, that is loaded, not used by an actor in the room ($72BF) and not the costume of the actor the player controls
Frees every sound, from 126 down, that is loaded and not in use ($753F), except sounds 3, 4 and 5
Frees every global script, from 154 down, that is loaded and not running or locked ($76F4)
Copies $4B/$4C bytes from $4D/$4E to $4F/$50, a page at a time from the bottom up, which is safe when a block moves down

Start-up: clears the variable area $679D-$77D4 ($1038 bytes) with fill_bytes, then makes the whole heap one free block: a header at $77D5 giving its size, $502B bytes (to $C7FF), and the heap's pointers at $FFEC-$FFF1 all pointing at it
Stores X into the $1B/$1C bytes from the pointer at $19/$1A on; the count must not be zero

Once a pass of the main loop: calls $624B, only an RTS, then runs every slot from 1 to 19 whose status is 2 (running): makes it current, finds its script with find_script_base and runs it until it yields; the slot number counts in $FC29, which it leaves at 1

The interpreter: fetches the current slot's next opcode with fetch_script_byte, keeps it in current_opcode ($FC2C), looks up its handler in the tables under the I/O chips ($D100 low bytes, $D000 high bytes; the RAM is banked in, as it is in all of play), calls $624A, which is only an RTS, and calls the handler through the JSR at $4C74, whose address it has just written; loops until a handler sets current_slot ($6851) negative
The handler's address is written into this JSR's operand by $4C68 and $4C6E

After something may have moved the heap (a load, a compaction): saves the current slot's offset with save_script_offset, finds its script's address again with find_script_base and rebuilds the script pointer with set_script_pointer
Builds the address of the current slot's next byte (its base, script_base $FC2A/$FC2B, plus its offset, $6866/$6852) into the operand of fetch_script_byte's LDA; nothing when no slot is current
The reverse of set_script_pointer: takes the base off the address in fetch_script_byte's operand and keeps the slot's offset in $6866/$6852
Steps over one byte of the script, then falls into fetch_script_byte

Reads the current script's next byte through the absolute address in its own operand ($4CBF/$4CC0), which set_script_pointer builds, and steps the address on; every script byte the interpreter reads comes through here

Sets script_base ($FC2A/$FC2B) for the current slot from what kind of script it runs (the low six bits of $68CA): 2, a global script, at its resource's address from $7659/$75BE plus 4 for the resource header; 1, the room's own script, at the room's address ($73BA/$737F for the current room); 0, an object's verb script, at the inventory object's address ($67D9/$6815). A script that is not in memory stops the slot (stop_current_slot); any other kind is a fatal error, code 8
Fatal error: keeps the code in $C9, banks the chips in and changes the border colour for ever; $4D2B never returns
Frees the current slot (status 0) and leaves no slot current
Frees every slot that runs a room script (kind 1): called when the room changes

Stops global script A wherever it runs: frees every running slot (but slot 0) whose script it is, clears its count in $76F4 but for the lock bit, and marks each nested call of it waiting in the call stack ($6225/$622F) as gone ($FF)

Starts global script A: stops it first if it runs (stop_script), loads it from the disk if it is not in memory ($2F27, then refresh_script_pointer), counts one more use in $76F4, takes a free slot (find_free_slot), sets it to the script's start with status 2 and kind 2, and runs it at once with run_nested
Returns in X the first free script slot from 1 to 19 (status 0); with none free, a fatal error, code 9
Fatal error 9, no free script slot: the border changes colour for ever

Runs slot X now, inside the current script: saves the current slot's offset, pushes its script number (or $FF when no slot is current) and kind onto the call stack at $6225/$622F (its depth in $6224), runs slot X until it yields, then pops the caller and makes it current again if it is still running; if it has gone, no slot is current
Redraws the inventory with redraw_inventory ($F380), with the chips banked in and the flag at $FF72 set while it runs, then banks the RAM back
Clears the 640 bytes of picture rows from $C850 and the same at $CC50: the room area of both screens

For the comparison opcodes: reads a variable's value (read_var) into $BD/$BE, then the opcode's second operand, a word or a variable (read_word_operand), into $6215/$6216, and compares them high byte first: carry set when the variable is the larger or equal, zero set when they are equal
Reads an operand that is a variable when bit 5 of the current opcode is set (read_var) and a byte in the script when it is clear; the value in $6215/$6216 and A
The same for bit 6 of the opcode
The same for bit 7 of the opcode: the commonest form, an opcode's first operand
Reads a variable number from the script and its value into $6215/$6216 (low bytes at $FE6E, high bytes at $FD6F); variables 14, 15 and 16 are indirect: their own value names the variable read
Reads an operand that is a variable when bit 5 of the current opcode is set and a word in the script, low byte first, when it is clear; the value in $6215/$6216
The same for bit 6 of the opcode
The same for bit 7 of the opcode
Reads a variable number from the script and makes the variable it holds the one the opcode's result goes to ($6217)
Reads the number of the variable the opcode's result goes to into $6217
Reads an object number (read_word_operand_80) and returns its byte in the object table at $6B47 (owner in the low four bits, state flags in the high four) with read_object_byte
Returns the byte for the object in $6215/$6216 from the object table at $6B47; the table's address is written into the LDA at $4F51, so write_object_byte can store back to it
Stores A back into the object table, at the byte read_object_byte read last (it copies that LDA's operand into the STA at $4F63)
Stores A, with a zero high byte, in the opcode's result variable (store_result at $5120)
Returns in Y the first free slot from 1 to 59 in the inventory table at $679D and keeps the highest used in $624C; with none free, a fatal error, code 10

The larger of the X and Y distances between two objects or actors, whose numbers are in $623B/$623C and $623D/$623E: finds each one's position with $08A4 ($FC18/$FC19) and returns the larger difference in A; $FF from $08A4 (not in the room) returns at once
For every slot from 19 down to 1 whose status is 1 (delayed), counts its three-byte delay ($68B6, $68A2, $688E) up by one; when it reaches zero the slot runs again (status 2)

Opcode $58, beginOverride: keeps where the script will go on (its offset after this opcode, $FF6D/$FF6E) and the slot ($FF70), so that a key press can skip a cut-scene to there; then steps over the jump that follows
Opcode $18, jumpRelative, and the jump that every condition opcode takes: reads a 16-bit offset and adds it to the script pointer
Opcodes $00 and $A0, stopObjectCode: a global script stops itself with stop_script, which ends every copy of it; any other kind of script frees its slot. No slot is current afterwards
Opcode $AE, waitForMessage: while a message is being shown (variable 3, $FE71, not zero) steps the script back onto this opcode and yields, so it runs again next frame

Opcode $4C, waitForSentence: returns at once when no sentence is queued ($094D is $FF) and the sentence script, global script 2, is not running ($76F6); otherwise steps back onto this opcode and yields
Opcodes $3B and $BB, waitForActor: reads an actor number; while that actor is walking ($FCF6 for its walk record, $FD56) steps back onto this opcode and yields
Opcode $80, breakHere, and how every wait yields: saves the slot's offset and leaves no slot current, so the interpreter loop returns
Opcodes $0A and $8A: the variable named by a variable gets a word or variable value
Opcodes $26 and $A6, setVarRange: reads a first variable and a count, then that many values, words when bit 7 of the opcode is set and bytes when it is clear, into consecutive variables
Opcode $2C: a variable gets a byte from the script
Opcodes $1A and $9A, move: a variable gets a word or a variable's value
Stores $6215/$6216 in the result variable ($6217)
Opcode $46: adds one to a variable
Opcode $C6: takes one from a variable
Opcodes $2A and $AA: adds a word or variable to the variable a variable names
Opcodes $6A and $EA: takes a word or variable from the variable a variable names
Opcodes $5A and $DA, add: adds a word or variable to a variable
Opcodes $3A and $BA, subtract: takes a word or variable from a variable
Opcode $28: goes on to the next opcode when the variable is zero, and takes the jump that follows when it is not
Opcode $A8: goes on when the variable is not zero, and jumps when it is
Opcodes $38 and $B8: goes on when the operand is less than or equal to the variable, and jumps otherwise
Opcodes $04 and $84: goes on when the operand is greater than or equal to the variable, and jumps otherwise
Opcodes $44 and $C4: goes on when the operand is less than the variable, and jumps otherwise
Opcodes $78 and $F8: goes on when the operand is greater than the variable, and jumps otherwise
Opcodes $08 and $88: goes on when the operand and the variable differ, and jumps when they are equal
Opcodes $48 and $C8: goes on when they are equal, and jumps when they differ
Opcodes $1D, $5D, $9D and $DD: reads an object and a mask of class bits; goes on when the object is in memory and has every bit of the mask in its byte 6, and jumps when it is missing or lacks one

Opcodes $62 and $E2, stopScript: reads a script number, 0 meaning the current slot's own; a global script stopping itself (in any slot but 0) ends as stopObjectCode does, and any other is stopped wherever it runs with stop_script
Opcodes $42 and $C2, startScript: starts the global script whose number is the operand (start_script), which runs at once, nested in this one
Opcodes $4A and $CA, chainScript: stops the script this slot runs, leaves no slot current and starts the script named by the operand in its place
The object state tests that go on when the bit in A is set in the object's byte (read_object_flags) and take the jump when it is clear
The tests that go on when the bit in A is clear and jump when it is set
Opcodes $0F and $8F: go on when bit 7 of the object's byte is clear (ScummVM's ifStateIntrinsicOn, whose jump is taken when the bit is set)
Opcodes $4F and $CF: go on when bit 7 is set (ScummVM's ifStateIntrinsicOff)
Opcodes $2F and $AF: go on when bit 6 is clear (ScummVM's ifStateLocked)
Opcodes $6F and $EF: go on when bit 6 is set (ScummVM's ifStateUnlocked)
Opcodes $1F and $9F: go on when bit 5 is set (ScummVM's ifStateTouchable)
Opcodes $5F and $DF: go on when bit 5 is clear (ScummVM's ifStateUntouchable)
Opcodes $3F and $BF: go on when bit 4 is clear (ScummVM's ifStatePickupable)
Opcodes $7F and $FF: go on when bit 4 is set (ScummVM's ifStateUnpickupable)
Clears the bits A leaves clear in the object's byte: ANDs it with A and writes it back
Sets the bits of A in the object's byte
Opcodes $07 and $87: sets bit 7 of the object's byte (in the room, an object that shows) and has the room redrawn ($CBC3 = $C8, and the list of objects to draw, $33BA, emptied)
Opcodes $47 and $C7: clears bit 7 and has the room redrawn, as op_set_state_80
Opcodes $27 and $A7: sets bit 6 of the object's byte
Opcodes $67 and $E7: clears bit 6
Opcodes $57 and $D7: sets bit 5
Opcodes $17 and $97: clears bit 5
Opcodes $37 and $B7: sets bit 4
Opcodes $77 and $F7: clears bit 4

Opcodes $05, $25 ... $E5, drawObject: reads an object, an X and a Y (each a byte or a variable, by bits 6 and 5); when the object is in the room, an X of other than $FF moves it there (its walk-to point moves by the same amount), it goes on the list of objects to draw ($33BB, counted in $33BA), every other room object of the same position and size loses bit 7, and this one gets it

Opcodes $50 and $D0, pickupObject: when the object is in the room, copies its record (its size in its first two bytes) into a new block in the heap ($D472), marks the copy (byte 2 = 1), files it in a free inventory slot ($679D numbers, $67D9/$6815 addresses; the slot goes in byte 3), gives the object to the current actor (variable 0) with bits 7 and 5 set, has the room redrawn and redraws the inventory
Opcode $CC, pseudoRoom: reads a room number, then a list of bytes ended by zero; each with bit 7 set makes that room number (less $80, the index into $7265) stand for the first room

Opcodes $72 and $F2, loadRoom: reads a room number; unless it is the room already shown (current_room, $6903), calls $D61E and enters the new room with enter_room ($2A38); then finds the current script again (the heap may have moved) and has the room redrawn

Opcodes $24, $64, $A4 and $E4, loadRoomWithEgo: reads an object, a room and an X and Y; a room script stops running here; puts the current actor (variable 0) in the room ($FF9D), enters it, places the actor at the object's walk-to point facing back the way it came ($08D8, $216C), points the camera at it and makes it follow ($5B6C), clears the sentence ($5C65), sends the actor walking to the X and Y when they are not negative, and starts global script 5. An object that is not in the new room is fatal error 11
JMP $5554, after the fatal error's endless loop: never reached

For the bit-variable opcodes: reads a word and adds the operand (a byte or variable) to make a bit number; sixteen bits make each variable, so the variable is the number divided by 16 ($6247), the bit is the low three bits ($6249) and bit 3 chooses its low byte ($FE6E) or its high byte ($FD6F), whose table's address it leaves in $15/$16
Opcodes $1B, $5B, $9B and $DB, setBitVar: sets the bit when the value read is not zero and clears it when it is zero (the bit masks at $623F)
Opcodes $31 and $B1, getBitVar: the result variable gets 1 when the bit is set and 0 when it is clear
Opcodes $10 and $90, getObjectOwner: the result variable gets the object's owner, the low four bits of its byte in the object table

Opcodes $29, $69, $A9 and $E9, setOwnerOf: gives an object to a new owner (a byte or variable); an owner of 0 also takes it out of the inventory and frees its copy (remove_from_inventory); then redraws the inventory and finds the current script again
Looks for the object in $83/$84 among the inventory slots 59 to 1 and, when it is there, frees it with free_inventory_slot
For an object held in the inventory (find_object returns 0): frees its copy in the heap ($D480) and empties its slot in $679D, $67D9 and $6815
Opcode $D8, printEgo: prints the message that follows in the script as said by the current actor (variable 0), with print_message_common
Hands the script pointer to the message printer ($21BA) in $C7/$C8, which reads the text from the script, and takes back where it stopped
Opcodes $14 and $94, print: reads the actor who speaks (a byte or a variable) into $FC30, then prints the message that follows
Opcodes $34, $74, $B4 and $F4, getDist: the result variable gets the distance between two objects or actors, the larger of the X and Y differences (actor_distance)

Opcodes $66 and $E6, getClosestObjActor: measures from the object to each actor from variable 20 ($FE82) down to variable 19 ($FE81) and gives the result variable the nearest actor's number, or $FF when every distance is $FF
Opcodes $16 and $96, getRandomNr: the result variable gets a random number from the routine at $D754, given the operand as its limit
Opcodes $56 and $D6, getActorMoving: the result variable gets the actor's walking state ($FCF6 for its walk record); an actor with no walk record in this room gives 1
Opcodes $7C and $FC, isSoundRunning: the result variable gets the sound's entry in $753F without bit 7
Opcodes $68 and $E8, isScriptRunning: the result variable gets 1 when any slot from 1 to 19 runs the global script, and 0 when none does

Opcode $2B, delayVariable: puts the slot to sleep (status 1) for as many counts of count_script_delays as the variable's value plus one: its three-byte delay counter is set to minus that, and counts up to zero; then yields
Opcode $2E, delay: the same with the three-byte count taken from the script, already as the negative number the counter counts up from
Opcodes $3C and $BC, stopSound: stops the sound named by the operand ($3E52), with the chips banked in
Opcodes $02 and $82, startMusic: makes sure the sound resource is in memory ($2EE4), then calls the music code at $C304 with its number, with the chips banked in, and finds the current script again
Opcodes $1C and $9C, startSound: reads the sound's number and starts it with start_sound

Starts sound A: sets bit 7 of $FC31 while it works, stops the sound if it is playing (stop_sound, chips banked in), makes sure its resource is in memory (load_sound), puts it on the list to begin at the next frame (queue_sound), clears bit 7 again, keeps the number in variable 37 ($FE93) and finds the current script again
Opcodes $36, $76, $B6 and $F6, walkActorToObject: when the object is in the room, sends the actor walking ($1761) to the object's walk-to point ($08D8)
Opcodes $0E, $4E, $8E and $CE, putActorAtObject: places the actor ($216C), in the room it is in, at the object's walk-to point, or at X 30, Y 60 when the object is not in the room

Opcodes $0D, $4D, $8D and $CD, walkActorToActor: reads two actors and a distance; when both are in the room, writes the distance and its negative into $0933 and $0938 and sends the first actor walking to a point that far from the second ($0914, then $1761); otherwise it steps over the operands left
Opcodes $1E, $3E ... $FE, walkActorTo: sends the actor walking to an X and a Y ($1761), with no direction to face at the end ($FC1A = $FF)
Opcodes $3D, $7D, $BD and $FD, setActorElevation: sets the actor's height above the floor ($FFD1) and, when it is in the room, counts its redraw counter ($FD22) up by two
Opcodes $01, $21 ... $E1, putActor: places the actor at an X and a Y in the room it is in ($216C)
Opcodes $2D, $6D, $AD and $ED, putActorInRoom: moves the actor to a room ($FF9D); room 0 also places it at 0, 0 in room 0, taking it out of play
Opcodes $0B, $4B, $8B and $CB, setObjPreposition: when the object is found (object_preposition), puts the preposition number in the top three bits of its byte 12
Opcodes $6C and $EC, getObjPreposition: the result variable gets the object's preposition, the top three bits of its byte 12, or $FF when the object is not found

Opcodes $19, $39 ... $F9, doSentence: verb $FC empties the sentence queue and stops the sentence script (global script 2); verb $FB drops the last queued sentence and clears the sentence line; any other verb is queued at $0954 with its two objects ($095A/$0960, $096C/$0972). A last byte of 1 then runs it at once (run_verb_script), 2 copies it into variables 26 to 29 and shows it on the sentence line, and 0 leaves it queued
Empties the sentence queue ($094D = $FF) and stops global script 2, the sentence script
Opcode $AC, drawSentence: redraws the sentence line from variables 26 to 29 (draw_sentence_line)

Runs the verb script of the object in $094F/$0950 for the verb in $094E, as a sentence: finds the object, in the inventory or in the room; verb $FE stops that object's scripts instead; $FD and $FA mark the script's kind with bit 7 (and bit 6), which other code reads as a script that the sentence does not own. Takes the slot already running a script of that object, or a free one, looks up the verb in the object's verb table (find_verb_entry) and does nothing when it is missing; otherwise sets the slot to start there and, but for $FD, puts the verb and the two objects in variables 8, 9 and 10, then runs it at once (run_nested)
The verb find_verb_entry looks for

Looks up verb A in the object's verb table, pairs of verb and offset from its byte 15 to a zero; an entry for verb $FF matches any verb. Returns the entry's offset into the object's record, or 0 (zero set) when the verb is not there
For verb $FE: frees every slot from 19 to 1 that runs a script of this object (its kind, without bit 6, and its number match)
Sets bit 7 of the status of every script slot, but the current one, that is in use and whose kind lacks bit 6: a status with bit 7 set no longer counts as running
Clears bit 7 of every slot's status, so frozen scripts run again

Opcode $40, cutscene: keeps the interface's state ($FF71 in $FF74), the cursor's (variable 21 in $FF73) and the room ($FF75); sets variable 21 to 200, hides the verbs, the inventory and the cursor and freezes the other scripts (set_user_state, $0F), empties the sentence queue, clears the sentence, and keeps the current slot ($FF6F) with no override yet ($FF6D/$FF6E = 0)

Opcode $C0, endCutscene: clears variable 5 (the override) and what the cut-scene kept of the override and its slot, gives variable 21 back its value, sets the interface back as it was (set_user_state with the kept state and bits 0 to 2) and has the camera follow the current actor again ($5B6C)
Opcodes $32 and $B2, setCameraAt: sets the camera's mode ($CBC6) to 3 and moves it to the X column the operand gives ($CB82)
Opcodes $12 and $92, panCameraTo: sets the camera's mode to 3 and its destination ($CBC8) to the operand, for the camera code to move towards
Opcodes $52 and $D2, actorFollowCamera: makes the camera follow the actor named by the operand (camera_follow_actor), then finds the current script again
camera_follow_actor for actor A, then finds the current script again (the room may have been loaded)

Puts the camera in mode 2, following actor A ($CBC7): when the actor is in another room, enters that room ($D61E, enter_room) and puts the camera on the actor's X; then sets the camera there ($CB82) and counts every actor slot's redraw counter ($FD22) up by two, so all four are drawn again
Opcodes $60 and $E0, cursorCommand: reads a word; a low byte other than 0 becomes variable 21, the cursor's state, and the high byte goes to set_user_state

Changes the interface's state in user_state ($FF71) by the bits of A: bit 2 copies bits 5 to 7 (the sentence line, the inventory, the verbs) into it; bit 0 freezes the other scripts (bit 3 set) or lets them run again; bit 1 copies bit 4, the cursor shown or hidden, and sets $1161/$1162 to 1 when it is hidden and 0 when shown. Then clears rows 18 to 24, redraws the verbs ($F261) and the inventory ($F380) with the chips banked in, and redraws the sentence line
Fills screen rows 18 to 24 ($CED0, 280 bytes) with spaces ($20)
Empties the sentence: no objects or preposition in variables 27 to 29, and variable 26, the verb, back to variable 38's (the default verb, Walk to)
Opcodes $71 and $F1, getActorCostume: the result variable gets the actor's costume ($FF90)
Opcodes $03 and $83, getActorRoom: the result variable gets the room the actor is in ($FF9D)

Opcodes $43 and $C3, getActorX: the result variable gets the actor's X from its walk record ($FCE6) when it is in the room. For one that is not, it reads $FFB7 indexed by Y, which holds $FF, not by the actor: the read wraps round to $00B6
Opcodes $23 and $A3, getActorY: the same for Y ($FCEA); for an actor not in the room it reads $FFAA plus $FF, which wraps round to $00A9
Opcodes $06 and $86, getActorElevation: the result variable gets the actor's height above the floor ($FFD1)
Opcodes $7B and $FB, getActorWalkBox: the result variable gets the walk box the actor stands in ($FD06 of its walk record), or $FF when it is not in the room
Opcodes $63 and $E3, getActorFacing: the result variable gets the direction the actor faces ($FFDE)

Opcodes $09, $49, $89 and $C9, faceActor: when the actor is in the room, turns it towards the object or actor ($08A4): 1 when the target is to the right and 0 when it is to the left; within two columns, 2 when the target is lower on the screen and 3 when it is higher. The new direction goes in $FD16 and bit 7 of $FCF6 asks for the turn

Opcodes $11, $51, $91 and $D1, animateActor: reads an actor and an animation number ($FC1B). $FC-$FF stops a walking actor in the room ($1629); $F8-$FB sets the direction it faces to the low two bits at once ($208A); $F4-$F7 turns a walking actor to that direction (set at once for one not in the room); any other number starts that animation in the direction the actor faces ($208A)

Opcodes $70 and $F0, lights: reads a value (a byte or variable) and two bytes. With a last byte of 0 the value becomes variable 12, the lights; with 1 the value and the next byte set the flashlight's width and height ($27C9 and $27CB, with 40 and 16 less them and their halves at $27CA-$27CE). Then, with the chips banked in, clears both screens' room rows when bit 1 of the lights is clear (dark), sets the sprites' shared colours (black and light red when bit 0 is set, black and dark grey when it is clear) and has the room redrawn
Opcodes $54 and $D4, setObjectName: copies the zero-ended name that follows in the script over the object's name ($0720 finds it), with no check of its length, and redraws the inventory

Opcodes $22 and $A2, saveLoadGame: turns the picture off (video_off), sets variable 13 to $30, reads the result variable and an operand; 1 calls $0AD5 and anything else $0A53, whose answer goes in the result variable; then finds the current script again and turns the picture back on
Opcode $20, stopMusic: stops the music ($4332)

Opcodes $0C and $8C, resourceRoutines: reads a resource number and a byte whose high four bits give its type ($20 costume, $30 room, $50 script, $60 sound) and low four what to do: 1 loads it if it is not in memory ($2EA3, $2E2E, $2F27 or $2EE4); 4 calls $4753 with $FC14/$FC15 = $0000/$FF00; 0 does nothing; any other sets (odd) or clears (even) bit 7, the lock, of its entry in the use counts: $72BF costumes, $7344 rooms, $76F4 scripts, $753F sounds
Low four bits 0: a row of comparisons of X with 2, 3, 5 and 6, each of whose branches goes to the next instruction; it does nothing
Opcode $98, restart: leaves the room ($D61E), enters room 0, clears the interface rows, resets the stack and jumps back into the start-up at $0418
Opcodes $5C and $DC: does nothing
Opcode $6E: turns the picture and sprites off (video_off), as the scripts do around a disk access
Opcode $EE: turns the picture back on (video_on)
Opcodes $30 and $B0, setBoxFlags: reads a walk box and a value, and writes the value into the box's flags byte ($24DE finds it)

Opcodes $7A and $FA, verbOps: a first byte of 0 deletes the verb in a slot (a byte or variable): frees its name (free_name_block) and clears its number in $F149. Any other first byte is a new verb's number: then come its column and row, its slot, and a preposition; its name, which follows in the script, goes into a block of its own (copy_name_to_heap), and the slot gets its rows ($F0D9, $F0F5), its first and last columns ($F111, $F12D), its preposition ($F165) and its number ($F149)
Frees the heap block that holds name number X ($778F high bytes, $77B2 low bytes: the actors' names from 2, the verbs' from 15) and clears its entry

Copies the zero-ended name at the script pointer into a new heap block for name number $621B: frees the old one, measures the new (its length with the zero in $621A), takes a block four bytes longer ($D472), files its address, finds the script again, copies the name in after a four-byte header (the block's size, type 4 and the name's number) and steps the script past it. An empty name gets no block
Opcodes $33, $73, $B3 and $F3, roomOps: reads two values and a sub-opcode: 1 sets the camera's limits, variables 23 and 24; 2 sets the room's two shared background colours ($D022, $D023)

Opcodes $13, $53, $93 and $D3, actorOps: reads an actor, a value and a sub-opcode: 1 the actor's sound ($FF83); 2 its colour ($FF76), and a redraw when it is in the room; 3 its name, which follows in the script (name number actor + 2); 4 its costume ($FF90), taking the old one off and putting the new one on ($2946, $2977) when the actor is in the room; 5 its talking colour ($FFC4)
Opcodes $15, $55, $95 and $D5, actorFromPos: the result variable gets the actor at an X and a Y ($314B)
Opcodes $35, $75, $B5 and $F5, findObject: the result variable gets the object at an X and a Y ($318E), a word

Opcode $AB (ScummVM's switchCostumeSet): with 1, takes $500 bytes, five pages, off the top of the heap's last block (fatal error 4 when it is too small) and loads sound 1 into them ($2EE4, with $61EF set so the loader puts it there), then forgets the sound's entry in the resource tables, so the heap never moves it: the music player, at $C300. With 2, gives the five pages back
Opcodes $6B and $EB (ScummVM's dummy): fatal error 12; no script should use them
1 while op_music_memory loads the music player: the loader reads it ($D4E8)
Bit 8 of each walking slot's sprite X position (four slots)
Not zero while the slot's actor stands behind something in the room, so its sprite column is masked after each frame (mask_actor_sprite)
Each actor's costume number (13 actors), zero for none
Each actor's X position in the room, in character columns (13 actors)
Each actor's direction (13 actors): 0 left, 1 right, 2 towards the player, 3 away
The head of the heap's list of free blocks, laid out like a free block: a size of 4 ($FFEC/$FFED), then the first free block ($FFEE/$FFEF), $77D5 after init_heap
The first block on the list of free blocks ($FFEF high), the head's link
The last block on the list of free blocks ($FFF1 its high byte), after which a block that is freed is put
